name: How to Plan an Accessible Bathroom Modification for Long-Term Safety

step.name: Step 1: Assess mobility requirements and transfer points
step.text: Evaluate how the resident moves into the room, transfers to the toilet, and enters the shower. Take note of whether a walker, wheelchair, or caregiver assistance is currently needed or anticipated.

step.name: Step 2: Measure doorways and clear turning dimensions
step.text: Confirm the entry door provides sufficient width for mobility equipment and check that the interior layout allows an open turning space, ideally a 60-inch turning radius or a clear T-shaped footprint.

step.name: Step 3: Check plumbing layout and structural conditions
step.text: Inspect existing floor framing and subfloor depth to verify whether a true curbless, zero-threshold shower drain can be recessed properly. Evaluate the plumbing supply lines and venting to ensure they support relocating valves or fixtures if necessary.

step.name: Step 4: Install solid wood wall backing before closing walls
step.text: Secure structural wood blocking directly between wall studs around the shower, bathtub, and toilet zones. This essential framing reinforcement ensures future grab bars and wall-mounted shower seats hold firm under heavy loads.

step.name: Step 5: Install accessible fixtures, nonslip surfaces, and controls
step.text: Lay slip-resistant flooring, set a comfort-height toilet, install an accessible vanity with open knee clearance, and mount single-lever water controls and a handheld showerhead within seated reach. When Professional Guidance Helps Modifying subfloors, moving waste lines, and reinforcing framing require licensed trade skills and local building permits.
